clue.text: Terrible jolt on Shaw from Bragg hero

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad way, so the letters of the words that follow are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A dreadful shock delivered by Bernard Shaw to a character of Melvyn Bragg's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' shuffles JOLT ON SHAW into the name of the footballer in Melvyn Bragg's 1980 novel, 'Shaw' being a playwright only in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Melvyn Bragg's novel about a gifted Cumbrian footballer is this man, so he is a hero of Bragg's fiction.

clue.text: Illyrian Duke shows gold associated with vice ring

parts.note: OR is the heraldic word for gold
a vice is a sin, a moral failing
a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A duke from Illyria displays gold and keeps company with a criminal gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice ring' reads as a criminal gang, but the two words give separate pieces: SIN, then the ring-shaped O.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Twelfth Night is set in Illyria, whose ruling duke, in love with Olivia, bears this name.

clue.text: Great Spirit's 4 showed great spirit

parts.note: the 4 points to the answer at 4-down, an envoy; in Longfellow's poem the Great Spirit, Gitche Manito, sends this Ojibwe hero to his people as a prophet and he acts with courage

explanation.walkthrough: The '4' stands for the answer at 4-down, envoy: Longfellow's hero is the Great Spirit's messenger, and 'showed great spirit' plays on the same phrase for his courage.
explanation.definitionFit: In Longfellow's narrative poem the hero is sent by Gitche Manito, the Great Spirit, to guide and teach the tribes.

clue.text: Jamesian envoy

parts.note: Henry James wrote a late novel titled after Lambert Strether and the other emissaries sent to Paris; a single one of them is the envoy meant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jamesian' points to Henry James's 1903 novel The Ambassadors, whose title figures are envoys.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy is a diplomatic representative, and Henry James named a novel after such figures.

clue.text: Reportedly inform dramatist of bridge expert

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the word for inform counts only by its sound

parts.note: to inform someone is to tell them
John Ford was a Jacobean playwright, author of 'Tis Pity She's a Whore

explanation.surface: Someone apparently tips off a playwright about a man who knows all about bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge expert' suggests the card game, but it is the Scottish civil engineer Thomas Telford, builder of the Menai Suspension Bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford was a celebrated engineer who designed many bridges, canals and roads in Britain.

clue.text: Associated with the far by L.H. Myers

definitions.text: Associated with the far by L.H. Myers

parts.words: Associated with the far by L.H. Myers
parts.note: L.H. Myers wrote a novel set in Mughal India whose title pairs two words with 'and', the second being 'the Far'

explanation.walkthrough: L.H. Myers's 1929 novel is The Near and the Far, so the answer is the word joined to 'the Far' in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: In the title of Myers's novel the word stands beside its opposite, so it is the companion of 'the far'.

clue.text: Quixotic story (the butler did it)

parts.note: the detective-story catchphrase about the butler doing it here means Samuel Butler wrote it: a mock-heroic poem whose knight and squire copy Don Quixote

explanation.walkthrough: 'The butler did it' is the whodunnit cliché, but here Butler is Samuel Butler, the seventeenth-century satirist who wrote this poem modelled on Cervantes.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Butler's satirical poem follows a Presbyterian knight on Quixote-style adventures with his squire Ralpho.

clue.text: Spearhead of stout oeuvre

explanation.surface: The leading edge of a sturdy body of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like an adjective for sturdy, but it is Rex Stout, whose first Nero Wolfe mystery (1934) bears this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means iron of a lance, a spear's point, and it titles the first Nero Wolfe novel by the American writer Rex Stout.

clue.text: Unearth former Scottish philosopher

parts.note: ex- is the prefix meaning former, as in ex-wife
David Hume was the eighteenth-century Edinburgh philosopher

explanation.surface: Dig up a once-famous thinker from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: To unearth a body is to dig it out of the ground, as with a corpse taken from its grave.

clue.text: Source of Byzantine prose?

parts.note: Byzantine writing literally comes from Byzantium, the city later called Constantinople and today the largest city of Turkey

explanation.walkthrough: 'Byzantine prose' suggests convoluted writing, but the clue means writing from Byzantium itself, whose modern name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Byzantium became Constantinople and is now the Turkish city on the Bosphorus, so it is where Byzantine writing came from.

clue.text: Stravinsky's oriole?

parts.note: Stravinsky's 1910 ballet for Diaghilev is named after a magical bird; the American oriole has a bright flame-coloured plumage and shares the popular name

explanation.walkthrough: The Baltimore oriole is popularly called by the same name as Stravinsky's ballet, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Stravinsky's ballet is named after a glowing bird of Russian folklore, and the bright orange Baltimore oriole has the same folk name.

clue.text: Like Nevil Shute's secret

parts.note: Nevil Shute wrote a 1945 wartime novel whose two-word title ends 'Secret'; the first word describes that secret

explanation.walkthrough: Nevil Shute's novel is Most Secret, so the answer is the word that qualifies his secret.
explanation.definitionFit: In the title of Shute's novel the word means to the greatest degree, describing how secret the matter was.

clue.text: Easy hero

parts.note: Captain Marryat's 1836 naval novel is titled Mr ___ Easy, after its young hero Jack Easy, a junior naval officer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Easy' is not an adjective but Jack Easy, hero of Frederick Marryat's Mr Midshipman Easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Easy holds the junior naval rank named in the title of Marryat's novel, so the rank is his title.

clue.text: Ultra crisp version based on Holy Writ

indicators.note: a version is a rendering in another form, so the two words before it are given in a new letter order

explanation.surface: A very crunchy edition of a text grounded in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Version' asks for a rearrangement of ULTRA CRISP.
explanation.definitionFit: Holy Writ is the Bible, and something founded on its text is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Composer lacks colour (awful strain) ..

parts.note: something pale is wan, lacking colour

indicators.note: awful means terribly bad, so the word strain is mangled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A composer is washed out by the dreadful strain of his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer' is the definition at the start, not a would-be anagram signal; 'awful' scrambles only the word in the brackets, and the ellipsis leads on to 16-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was a sixteenth-century Italian writer of sacred polyphonic music.

clue.text: It is not rebellion itself which is noble but the — it makes "(Camus)

definitions.text: It is not rebellion itself which is noble but the — it makes "(Camus)

parts.words: It is not rebellion itself which is noble but the — it makes "(Camus)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word completes the quotation from Albert Camus about what rebellion requires of the rebel

explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks a missing word: Camus wrote that it is not rebellion itself which is noble but the demands it makes upon us.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation needs a plural noun meaning requirements or claims, the things rebellion asks of those who rebel.

clue.text: … while another makes billiards shot over tennis obstacle

indicators.note: in a down entry over means on top of, so the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a massé is a billiards stroke made with a near-vertical cue to swerve the ball
the net is the barrier across the middle of a tennis court

explanation.surface: Meanwhile someone else plays a swerve shot in billiards over a tennis barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 14-down: 'another' means another composer, here Jules Massenet, the French composer of the opera Manon.
explanation.definitionFit: Following on from the previous clue's composer, this word stands for a second composer, the Frenchman who wrote Manon and Werther.

clue.text: Everything one boy discovers: S. R. Crockett's Andrew

parts.note: all means everything, the whole lot
I is the Roman numeral for one
a son is a boy, someone's male child

explanation.surface: Everything one lad finds out about a hero of the Scottish novelist S. R. Crockett.
explanation.definitionFit: S. R. Crockett, a Scottish novelist of the Kailyard school, wrote about a lad of this surname named Andrew.

clue.text: Incursive types from Plomer

parts.note: William Plomer, the South African-born poet and novelist, published a 1934 novel titled The ___; incursive people are those who raid or encroach

explanation.walkthrough: William Plomer's 1934 novel is The Invaders, and invaders make incursions.
explanation.definitionFit: People who make incursions into a territory are raiders, and Plomer named a novel after them.

clue.text: Writer of screen versions of classics exploded a petard

definitions.text: Writer of screen versions of classics

indicators.note: something exploded is blown apart, so the letters of the words before it are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: A screenwriter of great novels blew up a bomb, hoist with his own petard.
explanation.walkthrough: A is kept as written; 'exploded' rearranges PETARD to DAPTER. A petard is a small bomb, so 'exploded' suits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who turns a classic novel into a film script reworks it for the screen, so is a person who adapts.

clue.text: Injured sheep travels to the Islands of The Blessed

indicators.note: something injured is damaged out of its true shape, so the word sheep is rearranged

parts.note: to ride is to travel on horseback or in a vehicle

explanation.surface: A hurt sheep makes its way to the happy isles of the afterlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Injured' rearranges SHEEP to HESPE, followed by RIDES.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these nymphs' garden lay at the world's western edge, and their name came to cover the Fortunate Isles of the blessed dead.

clue.text: Ballot opens very old theatrical exercise

indicators.note: the word opens takes the letters that open, the initial letters of each of the four following words

explanation.surface: A poll launches an antiquated drama workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opens' takes the first letter of each of 'very old theatrical exercise'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballot is the casting of a choice in an election, a voice given at the polls.

clue.text: Sacred books concealed in distant Rajasthan

indicators.note: the answer is tucked away inside the letters of the words distant Rajasthan, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: Holy scriptures kept hidden in a remote part of an Indian state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealed in' points to the letters running from the end of 'distant' into 'Rajasthan'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hindu and Buddhist esoteric scriptures of ritual and meditation go by this Sanskrit name.

clue.text: Ability to versify the Deutschland, say, or the Hesperus?

definitions.text: the Deutschland, say, or the Hesperus?

explanation.surface: Poetic talent is linked with two famous wrecked vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: Hopkins wrote The Wreck of the Deutschland and Longfellow The Wreck of the Hesperus, so each is a poet's ship, run together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of being a poet is a poet's craft and skill, and the two vessels both belong to poets through their famous poems.

clue.text: A large quantity, say, for obsequious clerk

indicators.note: say signals that the following word counts for its spoken sound, as if said out

parts.note: a heap is a pile, a large quantity of things

explanation.surface: A great deal, apparently, is paid out for a fawning office worker.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep is the fawning, 'ever so humble' clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Uriah Heep, the servile law clerk in David Copperfield, is a byword for obsequiousness.

clue.text: Gladiators' missiles

parts.note: the retiarius gladiator fought with a net and a three-pronged spear, and the US and UK nuclear submarine missiles bear the same name

explanation.walkthrough: The retiarius gladiator's three-pronged spear shares its name with the submarine-launched nuclear missiles.
explanation.definitionFit: The net-fighting gladiator carried a three-pronged spear, and Britain's submarine-launched nuclear missiles share that name.

clue.text: "— the patriotic gore / That flecked the streets of Baltimore" (James Ryder Randall)

definitions.text: "— the patriotic gore / That flecked the streets of Baltimore" (James Ryder Randall)

parts.words: "— the patriotic gore / That flecked the streets of Baltimore" (James Ryder Randall)
parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing verb opens a line of Randall's 1861 poem Maryland, My Maryland, calling for retribution for the Baltimore riot

explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks a missing word from Randall's poem, later Maryland's state song: 'Avenge the patriotic gore'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem demands retribution for blood shed in Baltimore in 1861, so the missing verb means to exact revenge for.

clue.text: Like Leconte de Lisle's tragic poems of the mountain

definitions.text: Like Leconte de Lisle's tragic poems of the mountain

parts.words: Like Leconte de Lisle's tragic poems of the mountain
parts.note: Leconte de Lisle led the French school of poets named after Parnassus, the Greek mountain sacred to the Muses, and wrote Poèmes tragiques

explanation.walkthrough: The French school of Leconte de Lisle was named after Parnassus, the Muses' mountain, so his Poèmes tragiques belong to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French poetic movement around Leconte de Lisle took its name from Parnassus, home of the Muses, so his verse is described by its adjective.
